msgs.author: TPI HQ Bot
msgs.title: Being fully invested feels like wisdom in a rally.
msgs.pub:
Being fully invested feels like wisdom in a rally.

Ovid tells how King Midas asked that everything he touched turn to gold.

The wish came true. Then he reached for bread and it turned to metal in his hand.

Retail near a top makes the same wish. Every dollar into the position.

It works for months. The account looks rich.

Then a bill arrives during a panic, and the only way to pay it is to sell at the low.

Cash looks dead in a rally. It is the bread.

Gold only counts if you can wait to sell it.

msgs.author: TPI HQ Bot
msgs.title: Your portfolio may still carry its names and none of its reasons.
msgs.pub:
Your portfolio may still carry its names and none of its reasons.

Plutarch tells of the ship of Theseus, kept by the Athenians for centuries.

Each rotten plank was replaced with a new one, until philosophers argued whether it was still the same ship.

Positions age the same way.

You bought for growth. Growth slowed, and now you hold for the dividend.

Every plank of the thesis has been swapped. The name on the hull stayed.

Fair enough, some theses should evolve.

Once a year I write each holding next to the reason I bought it. If the reason is gone, I judge it as a new buy at today's price.

msgs.author: TPI HQ Bot
msgs.title: Your sell rule is only as strong as your fear on the day you need it.
msgs.pub:
Your sell rule is only as strong as your fear on the day you need it.

Hume put it bluntly. Reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions.

He meant that reason never moves us alone. It serves what we already want.

Watch a trader in a drawdown. The analysis keeps finding reasons to hold.

The fear of booking the loss writes the research.

I like to think I am the exception. My old trades disagree.

So I write the exit before the entry, while I want nothing yet.

That is the only hour my reason works for me.

msgs.author: TPI HQ Bot
msgs.title: Perma-bulls have an answer for every red day.
msgs.pub:
Perma-bulls have an answer for every red day.

Voltaire wrote a character for them in Candide.

Pangloss lives through disaster after disaster, the Lisbon earthquake included, and still says all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds.

Rates up, buy the dip. Earnings miss, buy it again.

Sometimes they are right. Dips have paid for years.

Then one day the dip is a new trend, and the explanation sounds exactly the same.

A thesis that explains every outcome tells you nothing.

I want to know in advance which price would prove me wrong.

msgs.author: TPI HQ Bot
msgs.title: High profits are the most public secret in markets.
msgs.pub:
High profits are the most public secret in markets.

Everyone can see them. That is the problem.

When a sector earns far more than normal, new money builds new capacity.

The supply shows up later, right when late bulls are paying the top multiple.

The price of the product falls. The margins drift back to normal.

The stock was priced for the peak to last forever.

When everyone agrees a business prints money, I start counting the new competitors.

msgs.title: Every trader in a drawdown makes the same promise.
msgs.pub:
Every trader in a drawdown makes the same promise.

Get me back to even and I am done.

I have heard it many times. I have said it myself.

Nobody keeps it.

Back at even, the account looks fine again, and fine feels like permission.

A few dollars up, and the old itch asks for one more trade.

That promise is a painkiller. It wears off the day the pain stops.

msgs.author: TPI HQ Bot
msgs.title: Most traders spend the day guessing what other traders will think.
msgs.pub:
Most traders spend the day guessing what other traders will think.

A number comes out. Before anyone reads it, funds are already betting on how retail will react.

Then retail bets on how funds will react to retail.

Nobody is trading the fact anymore.

That is how a good report sinks a stock by lunch.

There is no floor under a guess about a guess.

I try to start with what the business earns, before I think about anyone's reaction.

msgs.author: TPI HQ Bot
msgs.title: The most boring habit in investing is the one that pays.
msgs.pub:
The most boring habit in investing is the one that pays.

Camus wrote about Sisyphus pushing his rock up the hill forever. It rolls down, and he walks back after it.

Camus said we must imagine Sisyphus happy.

Rebalancing feels like that. You trim what ran and add to what fell. Next quarter, again.

Retail hates it because nothing exciting ever happens.

The dull push is where the money comes from.

I have learned to like the walk back down the hill.

msgs.author: TPI HQ Bot
msgs.title: Every sharp operator becomes the mark one day.
msgs.pub:
Every sharp operator becomes the mark one day.

Daniel Drew spent years as the spider of the Erie pool. He trapped the flies.

Later, his old pupils invited him into a blind pool. Put in millions, close your eyes, trust us.

The game had changed under him. Shorting had stopped working.

His experience felt like an edge. It had become a blind spot.

When someone asks you to put money in and not look, you are the fly.

I only hold positions I can see from top to bottom.

msgs.title: Shorting a market because it feels too high is like ordering the tide back.
msgs.pub:
Shorting a market because it feels too high is like ordering the tide back.

The old English chronicle tells how King Canute set his throne on the shore.

He commanded the sea to stop. The water rose over his feet.

He did it to show his court that even kings have limits.

Perma-bears forget that part. They stand in the surf and shout at the chart.

The tide turns on its own clock, when the buyers run out.

I wait for the water to start going out before I bet against it.

msgs.author: TPI HQ Bot
msgs.title: Calling a top too early costs the same as being wrong.
msgs.pub:
Calling a top too early costs the same as being wrong.

In the Greek myth, Apollo gives Cassandra the gift of seeing what comes next.

Then he curses her. Nobody will ever believe her.

She warns Troy about the horse. They pull it inside the walls anyway.

Markets have their own Cassandras. Short sellers who saw the bubble a year before it broke, and blew up first.

The money goes to whoever is still standing when the horse opens.

So I keep my bearish bets small enough to survive being early.

msgs.title: Every model you trust was built on markets that already happened.
msgs.pub:
Every model you trust was built on markets that already happened.

You have to use the past. There is nothing else to study.

The future has not been tested yet.

A backtest that never lost in twenty years has never seen next year.

I size every system as if its worst drawdown is still ahead.

It usually is.

msgs.author: TPI HQ Bot
msgs.title: The last leg of a panic is rarely about fear.
msgs.pub:
The last leg of a panic is rarely about fear.

It is about margin calls.

Funds that must sell will sell, and brokers sell for retail on margin. Price stops mattering.

Then one morning nobody is left who has to sell.

The bounce starts with no news, and everyone hunts for a reason.

There is none. The forced sellers are simply gone.

That is why the first rally after capitulation feels wrong to buy.

Watch who still has to sell. The headlines come later.

msgs.author: TPI HQ Bot
msgs.title: Selling a winner too early hurts more than never owning it.
msgs.pub:
Selling a winner too early hurts more than never owning it.

You can watch a stock you never held run for months with no pain at all.

Sell one you owned, and every new high feels like money taken from your pocket.

The profit you booked stops counting. Only the missing part stays in your head.

That is how late bulls get made. They buy back higher just to stop the itch.

The trades that hurt me most were the ones I chased back.

Take the profit and close the chart.

msgs.pub: Hello my friends,   $FSLY  is a  $4.0B  edge cloud company whose revenue growth just sped up again, and the options crowd spent the week buying calls on it. Friday it dropped  6.5%  into the middle of its August value, which is where I want to meet it.  The options market is paying for the flow and ignoring the participation underneath. Tech breadth is thin, the index sits  1.0%  from its high while the share of stocks above their 50-day average fell from  51%  to  29%  in 20 sessions. So this is a name I want, at a price I pick, at half the size I would normally use.  {CHART : capture du screener Pullback de l'app avec  $FSLY  dedans}   The Setup  Fastly runs a network of servers placed close to the end user. Websites and apps use it to load faster, to block attacks, and to run code at the edge instead of in one central data center. Revenue grew  23%  year over year last quarter, up from  20%  the quarter before, so growth is accelerating on a  $4.0B  company. Fastly still loses money and burns free cash flow, so the only multiple is forward:  42.6x  the earnings the Street expects, and the valuation pillar of the app sits at  48/100 , middle of the road. The whole bet is that growth outruns the burn before the market loses patience. A growth recovery with a messy income statement, priced like one.  From a  $7.74  low,  $FSLY  ran to  $34.82 , then gave back  28.3%  of it. It closed Friday at  $24.96  ( - 6.5 %  on the session),  64%  of its 52-week range. The daily, weekly and monthly trends all still point up, and the uptrend is  28  sessions old. The stock swings about  12.1%  a day, which sets everything below.  {CHART : TradingView  $FSLY , layout Daniel, profil volume août + semaine}  I read this chart through volume, because on a stock that moves  12%  a day the only prices that mean anything are the ones where people actually traded. In August the auction built its value between  $22.30  and  $26.83 , with the heaviest trade at  $22.89 . Last week the value tightened to  $23.45  to  $25.05 . Friday's close at  $24.96  sits at the top of last week's value and just under  $25.00 , where dealers carry their biggest call position. That is a ceiling for now, and buying into a ceiling on a  12%  swing stock is how you get shaken out. The support the app sees is  $23.24 , and the gamma flip sits at  $22.50 : above it dealers dampen the moves, below it they amplify them. So I would buy the drift back toward  $22.89  to  $23.24 , where August did most of its business, and I would not chase the  $25.00  line. If it pays at  $30.02 , the supply left over from the 3-month high, you take the win and you do not wait for the old highs.   Fundamentals  Score:  50/100   The Good: revenue is growing  18%  a year, the balance sheet carries low leverage and scores  83/100 , and the growth pillar sits at  70/100 . The company is not borrowing to fund its growth.  The Bad: it is not profitable yet, the profitability pillar is at  17/100 , and it burns free cash flow every quarter.  15%  of the float is sold short, and the risk and dilution pillar sits at  31/100 .  The Street is on the bullish side:  10  analysts cover it, consensus buy, average target  $27.00 , about  8.2%  above the last close. The 50 is a strong balance sheet averaged with a business that still loses money.   The Sector  Technology is running on a narrow base. Only  14.5%  of S&P 500 tech names trade above their own trend, and that share is still thinning. Hello my friends,

$FSLY is a $4.0B edge cloud company whose revenue growth just sped up again, and the options crowd spent the week buying calls on it. Friday it dropped 6.5% into the middle of its August value, which is where I want to meet it.

The options market is paying for the flow and ignoring the participation underneath. Tech breadth is thin, the index sits 1.0% from its high while the share of stocks above their 50-day average fell from 51% to 29% in 20 sessions. So this is a name I want, at a price I pick, at half the size I would normally use.

{CHART : capture du screener Pullback de l'app avec $FSLY dedans}

The Setup

Fastly runs a network of servers placed close to the end user. Websites and apps use it to load faster, to block attacks, and to run code at the edge instead of in one central data center. Revenue grew 23% year over year last quarter, up from 20% the quarter before, so growth is accelerating on a $4.0B company. Fastly still loses money and burns free cash flow, so the only multiple is forward: 42.6x the earnings the Street expects, and the valuation pillar of the app sits at 48/100, middle of the road. The whole bet is that growth outruns the burn before the market loses patience. A growth recovery with a messy income statement, priced like one.

From a $7.74 low, $FSLY ran to $34.82, then gave back 28.3% of it. It closed Friday at $24.96 (-6.5% on the session), 64% of its 52-week range. The daily, weekly and monthly trends all still point up, and the uptrend is 28 sessions old. The stock swings about 12.1% a day, which sets everything below.

{CHART : TradingView $FSLY, layout Daniel, profil volume août + semaine}

I read this chart through volume, because on a stock that moves 12% a day the only prices that mean anything are the ones where people actually traded. In August the auction built its value between $22.30 and $26.83, with the heaviest trade at $22.89. Last week the value tightened to $23.45 to $25.05. Friday's close at $24.96 sits at the top of last week's value and just under $25.00, where dealers carry their biggest call position. That is a ceiling for now, and buying into a ceiling on a 12% swing stock is how you get shaken out. The support the app sees is $23.24, and the gamma flip sits at $22.50: above it dealers dampen the moves, below it they amplify them. So I would buy the drift back toward $22.89 to $23.24, where August did most of its business, and I would not chase the $25.00 line. If it pays at $30.02, the supply left over from the 3-month high, you take the win and you do not wait for the old highs.

Fundamentals

Score: 50/100

The Good: revenue is growing 18% a year, the balance sheet carries low leverage and scores 83/100, and the growth pillar sits at 70/100. The company is not borrowing to fund its growth.

The Bad: it is not profitable yet, the profitability pillar is at 17/100, and it burns free cash flow every quarter. 15% of the float is sold short, and the risk and dilution pillar sits at 31/100.

The Street is on the bullish side: 10 analysts cover it, consensus buy, average target $27.00, about 8.2% above the last close. The 50 is a strong balance sheet averaged with a business that still loses money.

The Sector

Technology is running on a narrow base. Only 14.5% of S&P 500 tech names trade above their own trend, and that share is still thinning. Over 20 sessions $XLK gained 4.1% while $FSLY gained 1.3%, so this stock is lagging a sector that is itself carried by a few large names. The app puts the tech bench in its oversold zone, which is the kind of washout I like to buy into, as long as I size for it.

{CHART : table /sectors de l'app}

Confluence

The Pullback screener flagged $FSLY on Friday, one day after the Breakout screener had it. The two read the same chart from opposite ends: the Breakout screener saw a stock pushing out of its base, the Pullback screener saw it come back to its levels the next day. A strong name that tried the top of its range and got pushed back to its value.

The options flow explains why the dip is worth a look. Over the last 5 sessions, $54.4M went to calls against $9.7M to puts, and the biggest call day was September 23 at $28.1M. Heavy call buying showed up on 4 of the last 10 sessions, so the buying keeps coming back. And the money stayed: open interest on the October 16 $25 calls rose by 1,765 contracts to 3,935, about $371K of premium that was held overnight instead of flipped.

The other side is real too. 43.1% of the volume printed off-exchange, and 66.3% of that was on the sell side. Insiders sold recently. The fund filings are a wash: D. E. Shaw and Millennium added, Citadel, Tudor and Renaissance cut, and quant funds rebalancing a position tells me nothing about conviction. So the call buyers are leaning one way, the off-exchange sellers the other, and the price is sitting inside the August value while they settle it. That is a positioning trade with a growth story behind it, and the size below reflects that.

Options Flow

Implied volatility is at 92.4% with an IV rank of 77, so options are expensive here. The confirmed October $25 calls are the cleanest read of what the buyers want: a move through the $25.00 wall within three weeks. I would rather own the stock at the August value than pay 92% implied for the same idea.

How To Play It

Conservative:

Entry: $22.89 to $23.24 (the August point of control up to support)

Stop: a daily close under $20.00 (under the dealers' put wall and the $20.24 most traded price of the last six months, the structure is gone)

Target 1: $30.02 (the supply left over from the 3-month high)

Target 2: $34.82 (the 52-week high)

From $23.24, that is roughly two dollars of upside to Target 1 for every dollar risked.

Aggressive:

Buy at $24.96, right under the $25.00 wall, with the same stop and the same targets. You risk about $5 a share to make about $5 to Target 1, so the math is worse and you are betting the call buyers push through the wall first. Half the size of the conservative line.

What Could Go Wrong

Earnings land on November 4, inside the holding window, and a growth company that misses its acceleration story gaps through any stop. 15% of the float is short and the stock moves 12% a day, so both directions run fast. And the index is making highs on fewer and fewer stocks, which is when a volatile mid cap tech name gets sold first. Max allocation 2%, and half of that while breadth keeps diverging.

Size accordingly.

Daniel

Hello my friends,

$HHH is a $4.3B land developer trading at 1.07 times its book value, and it just put in a 13.0% month off its 52-week low. My Short Squeeze screener flagged it today. 13% of the float is sold short, and the stock closed 3% above the support where I want to buy it.

The market prices $HHH like the rest of real estate, a sector where not one S&P 500 name trades above its trend. It misses what sits underneath: a growth pillar at 100/100, a price close to book, insiders buying and four funds with bigger lines. So I want this name on a pullback, at starter size, while the sector around it is still washed out.

The Setup

Howard Hughes builds master planned communities. The company buys large tracts of land, puts in the roads and utilities, sells lots to homebuilders and keeps the offices, shops and apartments that grow up around them, mostly in Las Vegas and Houston. Revenue in the last quarter came in 330% above the same quarter a year earlier. Land and condo sales book in lumps, so I treat that as one big quarter and I do not extrapolate it. The trailing P/E is 14.5. The Street expects earnings per share to fall from $4.94 to $1.02, and that puts the forward multiple at 70.1. Book value gives a cleaner anchor: $66.95 a share against a $71.75 price. Real estate is the most hated corner of the market right now, and that is where I look for bottoms. This is an asset play priced near book, with a squeeze attached.

The stock topped at $91.07 on November 26, 2025 and bled for most of a year into a $60.09 low on September 18. Since then buyers have taken it back. It closed at $71.75 (1.0% on the session), 38% of the 52-week range between $60.09 and $91.07. Over the past month it gained 13.0% while the S&P gained 0.4%.

I read this chart through volume. On a stock coming off a low, the prices that matter are the ones where buyers and sellers actually agreed. The bounce built its floor at $69.64, and Friday's close sits 3% above it. Resistance sits at $72.23, only 1% overhead. Above that, the supply from the 3-month high waits at $74.88. Everyone who bought up there is still underwater, and plenty of them will sell to get back to break-even. Buying $71.75 means paying for the bounce right under a ceiling, with the floor almost $10 away at the stop. I would let it drift back toward $67.29 to $69.64 and scale in there. I would only pay higher after a clean close through $72.23. If it reaches $74.88, take the win and do not wait for the old highs.

Fundamentals

Score: 71/100

The Good: the growth pillar scores 100/100, valuation 77/100 and balance sheet 75/100. At 1.07 times book, you pay $71.75 for $66.95 of assets on the books, so the price already sits close to what the company owns. The trailing P/E of 14.5 is low for a business growing its top line, and insiders bought recently.

The Bad: free cash flow is -$1.13B on Yahoo's numbers, against a $4.3B market cap. Building communities eats cash before the lots sell. The profitability pillar sits at 46/100 and risk and dilution at 59/100. Forward earnings of $1.02 a share are a fraction of the trailing $4.94. And 13% of the float is short, so plenty of traders bet on lower prices.

The Street covers it lightly. 3 analysts follow it with a consensus buy. Targets run from $79.00 low to $100.00 high, with the average at $89.67, 25% above the last close. Even the lowest target sits above my first target. The 71 averages a cheap, growing asset base with a business that burns cash to build it.

The Sector

Real estate is in a full washout. 0% of S&P 500 real estate names trade above their trend, and that reading is holding steady. $HHH gained 13.0% in a month inside that sector, so buyers are picking this name on its own merits. A bounce in a dead sector carries more risk, and I size it that way.

Confluence

My Short Squeeze screener flagged $HHH today. It is built to catch heavily shorted names that start moving against the shorts. The setup fits. 13% of the float is short, the stock beat the S&P by double digits over the past month, and every dollar higher squeezes the traders who sold near the lows.

The fund filings point the same way. In the last quarterly filing, Gotham Asset Management's line grew 129.2% in value to $42.77M. AQR's grew 109.8% to $12.97M, Marshall Wace's 248.9% to $10.67M and Balyasny's 1,488% to $4.29M. Those are changes in the value of each position, price moves included. Renaissance cut its line 75% to $1.62M and Tudor 97.6% to $200K. The funds with the bigger lines outweigh the ones that left, and insiders bought recently too.

The options market adds nothing here. On October 2, calls drew $33K of premium against $23K for puts. That is too light to read. 41.0% of the volume printed off-exchange, and that is mostly market-making, so it says nothing about intent.

That leaves a contrarian reversal with squeeze fuel underneath. Funds with bigger lines and insider buying supply the conviction. The short interest supplies the speed. The sector is the reason to stay small.

Conservative:

Entry: $67.29 to $69.64 (current pullback zone)

Stop: $61.33 (a weekly close below it says the bottom is not in)

Target 1: $74.88 (the supply near the 3-month high)

Target 2: $91.07 (the 52-week high)

From $67.29, you risk 8.9% to make 11.3% to Target 1, about 1.3 to 1. Starter size only, scaling in on the way down.

Aggressive:

Buy a daily close above $72.23, the resistance just overhead, with a tight stop under $69.64 support. The targets stay the same. From that entry, the upside to $74.88 and the risk to $69.64 come out about even. You are betting the shorts get squeezed through the ceiling first. Use a smaller size than the conservative line.

What Could Go Wrong

Earnings land on November 9, inside the holding window, and the Street already expects earnings to drop hard. A miss on land sales gaps through any stop. Real estate has nobody above trend, and a sector like that can keep sinking and drag even its strongest names down. A 13% short float moves the stock fast in both directions. Starter size, nothing more until the weekly close holds above $69.64.

Size accordingly.

Daniel

Hello my friends,

Someone opened 3,638 November puts on $CARG at the $31.00 strike and kept them through the close. It is the largest confirmed position among the near expirations on this name, and it bets against the stock.

The price keeps sliding while that money gets positioned. $CARG lost 13.6% in 21 sessions while the S&P 500 gained 1.5%, and it now sits just above support at $27.46.

The Flow. This Is Why You're Reading This.

$CARG closed at $28.31 (-1.5%). Here is what hit the 2026-11-20 chain.

Strike $31.00 (ITM) : the confirmed bet

  • Open Interest: 3,662
  • OI Change: +3,638 contracts
  • Volume: 2
  • Premium (mid): $3.50
  • Delta: -0.7031
  • IV: 45.3%

The buying happened on October 6. That session printed 7,291 puts against 2 calls on $CARG, and the open interest was still there at the next count. A same-day round trip leaves no open interest behind, so these contracts are held. 3,638 contracts held means roughly $1.27M in premium sitting on the position, controlling 363,800 shares, about $10.30M in notional exposure.

A delta of -0.7031 means the put gains that fraction of every $1 $CARG drops. An in-the-money put with that delta trades close to a short stock position with a capped loss. The buyer paid for direction. There is a second reading too. Several large funds grew their $CARG lines in the latest filing, and a fund that owns the shares buys exactly this kind of put to protect them.

Where The Dealers Are

The dealer map puts a ceiling right over the price. The put wall at $31.00 and the call wall at $32.00 both sit between the close and the 200-day average at $33.49. $CARG has to clear that band before any long thesis means much. The gamma flip sits far below at $24.00, under my stop.

  • Call wall: $32.00
  • Put wall: $31.00
  • Gamma flip: $24.00
  • Regime: amplifying

The regime reads amplifying. Dealer hedging adds fuel to moves in both directions. A break of $27.46 support can travel fast. A push through $31.00 can travel fast too, with 17% of the float sold short. I expect wide daily ranges into earnings and I size for them.

What The Options Market Is Paying

  • At-the-money IV: 50.5%, rank 62 over the past year
  • 25-delta skew: -0.0%

Options on $CARG cost a bit more than their yearly middle. A rank of 62 means buying here is fair, with no discount. The skew is flat, so puts carry no extra premium over calls despite the bearish flow. The $31.00 buyer got in at 45.3% IV, under the 50.5% at-the-money level.

Earnings land on November 4, 27 days out and inside the November window. The app shows no implied move for that print. I treat it as a gap risk either way and keep the size small.

Why Now

$CARG runs an online car marketplace, and the business earns well. The numbers:

  • Net margin: 17%
  • Return on equity: 53%
  • Free cash flow: $241.32M (Yahoo)
  • P/E: 15.5 trailing, 9.9 forward (trailing EPS $1.94)
  • Market cap: $2.1B, price to book 9.57
  • Street: 12 analysts, targets $39.0 low, $42.0 average, $46.0 high, the average 48.4% above the close

That profile draws funds in. The latest quarterly filing shows a split. The percentages below are changes in the VALUE of each line, price move included:

  • Renaissance Technologies: $22.97M (+96.3%)
  • Millennium Management: $21.15M (+742.7%)
  • Tudor Investment: $4.80M (+284.2%)
  • Point72: $2.89M (-32.0%)
  • AQR: $1.07M (-78.7%)
  • Bridgewater: $536K (-71.7%)

The price ignores all of it. $CARG peaked at $41.22 on August 7 and now trades 15.5% under its 200-day average. Daily, weekly and monthly trends all point down. The sector adds weight: only 5.0% of the S&P 500 communication services names trade above their trend, and that group is thinning in extreme fear. Cheap forward earnings on one side, a falling chart on the other. The put buyer bets the chart wins until the next report.

What They're Targeting

November 4, 2026: earnings. A miss or a soft guide pushes $CARG deeper below $31.00 and the put gains. A strong print that lifts the stock back over $31.00 strips the put of its intrinsic value.

November 20, 2026: expiry. The put keeps value at expiry only if $CARG closes below $31.00. It already sits there today, so the buyer needs the trend to hold for 6 more weeks.

How To Play It

Equity (conservative): Entry $28.31. Stop $25.76 (9.0% risk). Target $38.52 (36.1%). R/R 4.0. Size: Starter, cap around 2%.

The stop sits 2 ATR below entry, under the $27.46 support. A fill on a dip toward $27.46 improves the trade, and I would take it there first. The target is the next real resistance overhead. The trend and the options money both lean against this long, so it stays a starter.

Follow the flow (aggressive): The 2026-11-20 $31.00 put at $3.50 mid. It follows the buyer and bets against the share plan above. If $CARG breaks $25.76, the put gains at a delta of -0.7031, more as the delta climbs. If the stock closes above $31.00 on November 20, the put expires worthless. Max loss = the premium. Size: 1 to 2% of portfolio.

Best of both: The two plays point opposite ways, so I would never run them as two separate bets. Own the starter in shares and hold a small put position as insurance under it. A break of the stop then costs you less, and a squeeze leaves the shares to do the work.

What Could Go Wrong

A daily close below $25.76 breaks the setup and ends the trade. On the put side, volatility at a rank of 62 can deflate after the November 4 print, and theta eats the premium every day into November 20. The flow can also turn out to be a fund hedging shares it owns, and a hedge says nothing about direction.

Money on the table guarantees nothing. The buyer of 3,638 puts can be wrong, and a 17% short float can turn a good print into a run through $32.00. Size accordingly.

Daniel

$MAT trades at 8.1 times the earnings the Street expects, and over the last 21 sessions it gained 20.9% while the S&P 500 gained 2.7%. My Volume Leaders screener flagged it on October 9. I want to own it on a pullback toward $15.38, at half size, because earnings land on October 27.

The market still prices Mattel as a toy company with no growth left. It is missing the turn. The stock printed a 52-week low of $12.40 on October 1 and closed at $16.69 on October 9. Almost nothing else in consumer discretionary is going up, so the money picked this name on its own.

The Setup

Mattel designs and sells toys and owns the brands behind them: Barbie, Hot Wheels, Fisher-Price, and a licensing and entertainment business built on those names. It makes money. Return on equity sits at 20%, and the stock trades at 9.6 times trailing earnings and 8.1 times forward earnings on a $4.8B market cap. The valuation pillar of the app scores 97/100, which puts it near the cheapest end of anything I track. The multiple is low because the market stopped paying for toys after years of flat sales. That kind of pessimism tends to unwind fast once buyers come back, and consumer discretionary is now so washed out that a single name can lead without help from its sector. A cheap, profitable business the market had given up on, and the buyers are back.

The stock peaked at $22.48 on February 10 and bled for eight months, down to $12.40 on October 1. It closed at $16.69 on October 9 (0.7% on the session), at 43% of its 52-week range between $12.40 and $22.48. The whole year's decline has not been repaired. The bounce off the low is sharp, though, and it came on volume.

I read this chart through volume, because a stock coming off a 52-week low this fast only keeps the prices where real size changed hands. The rally pushed through $16.20, and the close at $16.69 sits 3% above that support, with the next resistance at $17.23, also 3% away. Everyone who bought between $17.23 and the February high at $22.48 is underwater, which means every push higher runs into holders who want to get out at breakeven. Dealers hold their biggest call position at $16.00 and their biggest put position at $14.00, and the gamma flip also sits at $14.00. Above that line their hedging dampens the moves. Below it their hedging amplifies them. So I would not chase $16.69. I would buy the drift back toward $15.38 in pieces and put the stop at $13.62, under the $14.00 line, where the structure is gone. If it pays at $19.32, take the win and do not wait for the February high.

Fundamentals

Score: 61/100

The Good: the valuation pillar scores 97/100. That rests on a trailing P/E of 9.6, a forward P/E of 8.1, and a price of 2.39 times book value of $6.99 a share. Return on equity is 20%. The risk and dilution pillar sits at 66/100, so the company is not printing shares to fund itself.

The Bad: the profitability pillar is at 41/100, the growth pillar at 51/100, and the balance sheet pillar at 50/100. The business earns money, but neither margins nor growth stand out. 14% of the float is sold short, which is a big short book for a company this cheap.

The Street leans bullish. 13 analysts cover it, consensus buy, with an average target of $18.15, about 8.8% above the last close. The range runs from $11.00 to $28.00, so they disagree a lot. The 61 blends a top valuation score with middling quality. You are paid for buying cheap here, and nobody is paying you for growth.

The Sector

Consumer discretionary has almost nobody left standing. Only 2% of the S&P 500 names in the consumer discretionary sector trade above their own trend, and that share has stopped falling without turning up. That is capitulation: the sellers have done most of their work.

$MAT beat the S&P by 17% over the past month inside that empty bench. The buying is about this name and this price, and a sector that turns up later would only add fuel.

Confluence

My Volume Leaders screener flagged $MAT on October 9. It is built to catch stocks where the volume backs the price move. A high-volume bounce off a 52-week low is the case it exists for. Price sat right at the $16.20 support on that day, so the screener caught the move and the level together.

The fund filings show who stands on each side. At the last quarterly filing, Ariel Investments held a $213.97M line, up 8.5% in value. Gotham Asset Management rose 185.9% to $33.33M, Bridgewater 412.8% to $3.08M, and Caxton 100.0% to $2.79M. On the other side, PRIMECAP's $409.54M line fell 5.1% in value, Southeastern's $171.04M fell 8.1%, AQR's fell 27.1% and Millennium's 33.8%. These are changes in position value, rally included, and they do not count shares bought. 9 tracked funds trimmed in total.

The two largest value holders shrank while smaller and faster funds grew their lines. Patient sellers still sit above the price, and short-term money is pushing it up into them. That makes this a trend trade off a low. I buy it on dips into support. A breakout against that supply needs proof first.

Options Flow

On October 9, $606K went to calls against $522K to puts, 54% on the call side, on 7,437 call contracts against 3,907 puts. Over 5 sessions the net premium leans to calls, at $4.53M. The cleanest read sits in the November 20 $17 calls. Open interest rose by 819 contracts to 1,310, about $98K of premium held overnight and $1.37M of notional. That position bets on a push through $17.00 before an expiry that spans the October 27 report.

The put side is still open. 1,004 of the November 20 $16 puts traded against open interest of 39, about $60K of premium. The next open interest update will show if the position was kept or closed inside the session. With earnings inside that window, it reads like a hedge until proven otherwise. Implied volatility at the money sits at 51.7%, so options are not cheap. I would rather own the stock near $15.38.

How To Play It

Conservative:

Entry: $15.38 to $16.20 (current pullback zone)

Stop: $13.62 (a daily close under it, below the $14.00 put wall and gamma flip, breaks the setup)

Target 1: $19.32 (the next real resistance, about 25.6% above entry)

Target 2: $22.48 (the 52-week high)

From $15.38, you risk 11.4% to make 25.6%, about 2.2 dollars of upside for every dollar risked. Scale in, half size, and cap the position around 3%.

Aggressive:

Buy at $16.69 now, with the same stop and the same targets. You risk more per share than you stand to make to Target 1, so the math is worse. You are betting that the $17 call holders push price through $17.23 before any pullback comes. Use half the size of the conservative line.

What Could Go Wrong

Earnings land on October 27, 15 days out and inside the holding window, and a miss gaps through any stop. 14% of the float is short, so the stock can run hard in both directions. And the lowest analyst target sits at $11.00, below the stop, so some of the Street sees the October low as unfinished business.

Size accordingly.

Daniel

Hello my friends,

$MAT trades at 8.1 times forward earnings and has risen 20.3% in 21 sessions, while the S&P 500 gained 2.3%. I want to own the trend on a dip toward $16.20, and I want to own it at starter size, because earnings land on October 27.

The market prices Mattel like a toy maker in a dead sector. Consumer discretionary is in its fear zone, and only 5.7% of the S&P 500 names in it trade above their trend. The options market noticed the rebound first: call premium is running 2.5× a normal day. The stock is already moving, and the sector around it is still in fear.

The Setup

Mattel makes toys: Barbie, Hot Wheels, Fisher-Price, UNO. Revenue rose 10% last quarter against the same quarter a year earlier. The stock trades at 9.6 times trailing earnings and 8.1 times forward, with the Street expecting earnings per share to climb from the trailing $1.33. On valuation, the app scores it 97/100, close to the top of the scale. The multiple is low because the sector is hated, and the holiday quarter is the one that makes or breaks a toy company's year. A cheap brand name priced for a bad Christmas.

The stock peaked at $22.48 on February 10 and bled for eight months, down to $12.40 on October 1. From there it turned hard. It closed Tuesday at $16.88 (0.7% on the session), 44% of the way up its 52-week range. It now sits 7.1% above its 200-day average of $15.76, so the long trend has turned back up.

I read this chart through volume. A stock that fell from $22.48 to $12.40 left trapped buyers at every level on the way down, and the levels where they traded are where they will want out. Everyone who bought the February high is still underwater, and every rally toward their entry price gives them a chance to sell at breakeven. The first of those levels is $17.23, right above the close. Support at $16.20 sits 4% below, so buying here puts you closer to the sellers than to the buyers. Dealers hold their largest call and put positions at the same strike, $16.00. Above the $13.00 gamma flip their hedging dampens moves, so the price tends to get pulled back toward $16.00. I would buy the drift into $16.20, where the October bounce has to prove it holds, and I would not chase the push into $17.23. If it pays at $19.55, the next real resistance, you take the win and do not wait for the February high.

Fundamentals

Score: 61/100

The Good: valuation is the pillar that carries the score at 97/100. Return on equity runs at 20%, which is high for a business priced under 10 times earnings. The market cap is $4.8B, and the risk and dilution pillar sits at 66/100, so the share count is not the problem.

The Bad: profitability scores 41/100, growth 51/100, and the balance sheet 50/100. The cash flow picture is mixed. Yahoo puts free cash flow at $425.32M, while the app's filing-based read flags it as burning free cash flow. And 14% of the float is sold short.

The Street leans bullish. 13 analysts cover it, consensus buy, average target $18.15, about 7.6% above the last close. The range runs from $11.00 to $28.00, which tells you nobody agrees on the holiday quarter. The 61 averages a stock priced for disaster with a business whose margins are only middling.

The Sector

Consumer discretionary is sitting in extreme fear. Only 5.7% of the sector's S&P 500 names trade above their own trend, and that share is holding steady with no sign of recovery yet. $MAT is rising while almost everything around it is not. Strength that holds up inside a bench this thin is the kind I want to own, as long as I keep the size small.

Confluence

The app leans long on $MAT, and the reasons are the price and the money. Over 21 sessions the stock gained 20.3% against 2.3% for the S&P 500, and it is holding above its 200-day average. That is a trend-following setup, built on a stock that already turned. Every one of those gains came after the October 1 low, so the move is young.

The options money points the same way. On Monday, October 12, calls took $1.83M of premium against $1.05M for puts, so 64% of the money sat on the call side. Over 5 sessions, net premium came to $4.69M. Someone is paying up for upside ahead of the print.

The fund filings split. At the last quarterly filing, Bridgewater's line rose 412.8% in value and Ariel's $213.97M line rose 8.5%. On the other side, PRIMECAP's $409.54M line fell 5.1% in value and Millennium's fell 33.8%. The large value holders trimmed, a few macro and quant funds added, and price changes drive part of those numbers. So the long-term owners are not chasing this bounce. That makes it a trend trade on fresh money, and the size below reflects it.

The biggest buy-zone problem is the one I flagged in the chart: the price sits closer to resistance than to support. The confluence is real, and the entry still has to come to me.

Options Flow

Implied volatility at the money is 46.9%, and the 25 delta skew is flat at 0.7%, so puts carry no real premium over calls. Among the near expiries, the contract where positions grew is the November 20 $15 put. Open interest rose by 99 to 187, about $3K of premium covering 9,900 shares, or $167K of notional. That is small, and it sits just under the $15.09 stop and after earnings. Someone is holding cheap protection through the print, which is what I would expect from a long who wants to stay in.

How To Play It

Conservative:

Entry: $16.88 to $16.20 (current pullback zone)

Stop: $15.09 (a daily close below it breaks the setup and ends the trade)

Target 1: $19.55 (the next real resistance)

Target 2: $22.48 (the 52-week high)

The closer you fill to $16.20, the better the math, because the stop stays where it is and the target gets farther away.

Aggressive:

Buy at $16.88 now, with the same stop and the same targets. You risk 10.6% to make 15.8% to Target 1, about 1.5 dollars of upside for each dollar risked. You are betting the call buyers push it through $17.23 before it ever comes back to $16.20. Starter size, capped around 2%.

What Could Go Wrong

Earnings land on October 27, in 13 days, inside the holding window, and a toy company that guides the holiday quarter down gaps through any stop. 14% of the float is short, so the moves run fast both ways. And the sector is still in extreme fear, so one bad consumer print can drag a name that has rallied this far straight back down. Cap it at 2%.

Size accordingly.

Daniel

Hello my friends,

$MAT is a $4.9B toy maker that trades at 8.1x forward earnings. Over the last 21 sessions it gained 29.2% while the S&P 500 gained 0.1%. My Volume Leaders screener flagged it on Friday, and the options money is buying calls that expire after the October 27 report. I want this name on a pullback, at half size.

The market is pricing a rebound off the $12.40 low of October 1. It misses the timing. Earnings land in 8 days, Friday's close sits just under the supply at $17.32, and 10 of the funds I track trimmed at their last filing. Buying here means paying the top of the move with a binary event attached.

The Setup

Mattel makes Barbie, Hot Wheels, Fisher-Price and UNO, and sells them through the big retailers and through licensing. The stock trades at 9.6x trailing earnings and 8.1x forward, because the Street expects earnings per share to grow from $1.33. Return on equity is 20%, and the shares trade at 2.46x a book value of $6.99 per share. A multiple that low prices a business in decline, and the October 27 report will test that before the holiday season. Consumer discretionary is washed out, and cheap names in a washed-out sector are usually the first to get rerated. $MAT is a cheap business in a hot run, and I want to pay less for it.

$MAT topped at $22.48 on February 10 and bled down to $12.40 on October 1. Then it turned hard. Friday it closed at $17.20 (-0.7% on the session), 48% of its 52-week range between $12.40 and $22.48.

I read this chart through volume, because a stock that runs this fast leaves thin trade behind it, and price tends to fall back through thin trade. Everyone who bought above $17.32 since February is still underwater, and that supply starts at $17.23. Friday's close at $17.20 sits right under it, just above $17.00, where dealers carry their biggest call position. The first support is $16.35, and below it sits $16.00, the dealers' put wall. I would not pay $17.20 into a ceiling 8 days before earnings. I would buy the drift back to $15.85 to $16.35 and scale in. If it tags $17.32 from there, you take the win and you do not wait to see whether the February buyers let it through.

Fundamentals

Score: 61/100

The Good: the valuation pillar scores 97/100, the strongest part of the score. 9.6x trailing earnings and 20% return on equity is a profitable business at a low price. Yahoo puts free cash flow at $425.32M, against a $4.9B market cap. Risk and dilution score 66/100.

The Bad: profitability sits at 41/100 and the balance sheet at 50/100. The app reads the SEC filings and flags free cash flow burn, which contradicts Yahoo's number, so I want the October 27 cash flow statement before I size up. 14% of the float is sold short.

The Street leans bullish. 13 analysts cover it with a consensus buy and an average target of $18.15, about 5.5% above the last close. Targets run from $11.00 to $28.00, so the analysts disagree as much as the cash flow sources do. The 61 is a stock priced near the floor, averaged with margins and cash flow that still have to prove themselves.

The Sector

Only 11% of the S&P 500 consumer discretionary names trade above their own trend, so the sector bench is oversold. That share has started to widen again. $MAT gained 29.2% while its sector sat this low, which makes it a leader coming out of a washout. Leaders like that are the ones I buy on the first pullback.

Confluence

The Volume Leaders screener flagged $MAT on Friday. That screener is built to catch moves that heavy volume backs, and this one came with a 29.2% run against a flat S&P 500. Strength like that pulls in momentum money, and the momentum money shows up in options first.

The fund filings show who supplied the shares. At the last quarterly filing, Ariel Investments' position grew 8.5% in value to $213.97M, Gotham's grew 185.9% to $33.33M and Bridgewater's grew 412.8% to $3.08M. Those are changes in the value of each position, and part of each move is the price itself. On the other side, PRIMECAP's position fell 5.1% to $409.54M, Southeastern's fell 8.1% to $171.04M, and Millennium and AQR cut by 33.8% and 27.1%. The two largest holders trimmed at the margin, and a deep value shop added.

The off-exchange print tells me nothing either way. 28% of the volume traded off-exchange and 59.8% of that was marked short, which is mostly market makers filling orders. So value money holds the floor, momentum money is pushing the price, and the large holders sell into strength. That mix makes this a positioning trade into earnings with a valuation floor under it, and the entry should come from the floor side.

Options Flow

On Friday $691K of premium went to calls against $162K to puts, so 81% of the money sat on the call side. Volume ran 7,370 calls to 3,552 puts, and net premium over five sessions came to $5.33M. The cleanest read is the November 20 $17 calls. Open interest rose by 569 contracts to 2,608, about $65K of premium held overnight, controlling 56,900 shares. Those calls expire after the October 27 report, so the buyers are paying for the earnings move. The November 20 $21 calls traded 250 contracts against open interest of 21, and we will know tomorrow whether that money stayed. Implied volatility sits at 50.8%, and I would rather own the stock at $15.85 than pay that for the same idea.

How To Play It

Conservative:

Entry: $15.85 to $16.35 (current pullback zone)

Stop: $14.04 (a daily close below it breaks the setup)

Target 1: $17.32 (the supply under the 3-month high)

Target 2: $22.48 (the 52-week high)

From $15.85 you risk 11.4% to make 9.3% at Target 1, about $0.80 of upside per dollar risked. That is thin. Target 2 carries the trade, so the size stays at half, capped around 3%.

Aggressive:

Wait for a daily close above $17.32 and buy the break, with the same $14.04 stop and $22.48 as the target. You pay more per share and your stop sits further away, so you are betting the call buyers clear the February supply. Half the size of the conservative line.

What Could Go Wrong

Earnings on October 27 fall inside the holding window, and a gap can jump straight through $14.04. 14% of the float is short, so the stock can run hard in either direction. The cash flow question is still open, and none of the screeners can see a weak holiday order book.

Size accordingly.

Daniel

Hello my friends,

The shares bounced 1.6% to $107.10 the next day. They still trade 19.2% under their 200-day average and far below the $170.19 high of February 9, so the chart still points down while the options money leans long.

The Flow. This Is Why You're Reading This.

$JBTM closed at $107.10 (1.6%). Here is what hit the near-dated chain.

The big print came a day earlier. On October 20, call premium reached $2.69M against $0 in puts, with 2,689 calls traded and zero puts. That is 31.7 times a normal day of call premium. Over 5 sessions the net still sits at $2.68M on the call side, so the money stayed in after the first day.

Strike $100.00 (OTM) : the unconfirmed signal

  • Volume: 77
  • Open Interest: 76
  • Vol/OI: 1:1
  • Premium (mid): $3.30
  • Delta: -0.2739
  • IV: 47.3%

This is the November 20 $100 put, and it bets the other way. It was the contract that stood out among the near expirations on October 21. The volume is there, but the open interest has not updated yet. If OI climbs tomorrow, someone held a new position overnight. If it stays flat, someone bought and sold inside the session. A delta of -0.2739 means the put gains about a quarter of each dollar $JBTM drops. It covers 7,700 shares, or $825K of notional. Next to $2.69M of calls, a position this small looks like protection on a long position more than a bearish call. About $25K changed hands here.

Watch the OI update tomorrow. That is the tell.

Where The Dealers Are

Dealers hold their biggest call exposure at $105 and their biggest put exposure at $100. The gamma flip also sits at $105. On October 21 the stock closed above that level. Holding above $105 keeps the bounce alive. A slip back under it brings $100 into play fast, and the stop sits just above that.

  • Call wall: $105.00
  • Put wall: $100.00
  • Gamma flip: $105.00
  • Regime: amplifying

The app reads the regime as amplifying. In that regime dealer hedging adds to the move, so the next sessions can travel farther than usual in whichever direction breaks first. Above $105, that pushes the bounce along. Below $100, the same hedging speeds the drop toward the stop.

What The Options Market Is Paying

  • ATM IV: 45.3%
  • 25-delta skew: -2.2%

A 45.3% implied vol prices big swings. That fits a stock that fell from $170.19 to $102.97 this year. I have no one-year rank for this vol today, so I cannot say if it is cheap or rich against its own history. The skew is small at -2.2%, so nobody is paying a panic price for crash protection. At this vol a call buyer needs the stock to move soon to beat time decay. That pushes me toward shares for the core of the trade.

Why Now

$JBTM is JBT Marel, a $5.6B maker of food and beverage processing equipment. The valuation is where the story starts:

  • Trailing P/E: 28.2
  • Forward P/E: 11.3, with EPS expected to more than double from $3.69
  • Price to book: 1.24, on a book value of $86.54 per share
  • Revenue: +5% last quarter against the same quarter a year earlier
  • Free cash flow: $341.06M (Yahoo)
  • Street: 8 analysts, targets $118.00 low, $167.06 mean, $210.00 high

The lowest analyst target sits above today's price. The mean implies 56% upside. The forward multiple of 11.3 shows how much earnings growth the Street expects, so the price is betting that growth never shows up.

The funds split at their last quarterly 13F filing. The Adage Capital line grew 52.1% in value, First Eagle 51.7% and Baron 13.5%, and Balyasny opened a new line. Marshall Wace cut its line by 31.3% in value and Point72 by 96.6%. These percentages measure the value of each line, price moves included, so they say less about share counts than they seem to.

The sector gives no help. Only 5.4% of S&P 500 industrials trade above their long-term trend, and the bench sits in extreme fear. Over 21 sessions $JBTM lost 5.5% while the S&P stayed flat.

That gap makes the trade. The fundamentals point to a stock priced for failure, and someone bought calls on the day of the low. Price still says the trend is down. As long as that holds, I size small.

What They're Targeting

My data holds no earnings date or other dated event before the November 20 expiry. The one date that counts is the expiry itself.

November 20: the $100 put expires. If tomorrow's OI shows it was held, the buyer wants protection through that date, right at the dealers' $100 put wall.

How To Play It

Equity (conservative): Entry $107.10. Stop $100.85 (5.8% risk). Target $132.08 (23.3%). R/R 4.0. Size: Starter, cap around 2%.

Resistance at $109.22 sits close overhead, and support at $103.26 sits below. A dip to $103.26 gives a cheaper fill against the same stop. I would take that fill if the market offers it before I get filled at $107.10.

Follow the flow (aggressive): The October 20 call money left no confirmed contract in the near-dated chain I can see. The one contract that showed up is the November $100 put, which bets the other way. I do not buy options on a signal I cannot price. If tomorrow's OI shows a call position held overnight, that contract becomes the trade, and the max loss is the premium. Size: 1 to 2% of portfolio.

Best of both: I hold shares as the core at Starter size, with the stop at $100.85. A call kicker comes only after the OI confirms. It takes a small slice of the 2% cap and never adds to it.

What Could Go Wrong

A daily close below 100.85 breaks the setup and ends the trade. The stock sits under its 200-day average and lags the S&P, and the October 20 buyers may simply be early. Vol at 45.3% can deflate if the bounce stalls, and that hurts any option held. On a November 20 expiry, theta takes a larger bite every week. The call flow could also be a hedge against a short stock position, and the $100 put could be someone protecting a long. Either case would leave less directional conviction behind the flow than it seems.

Money on the table guarantees nothing. The big buyer can be wrong, and the trend is still against them. Size accordingly.

Daniel

Hello my friends,

Somebody paid $115.10M for $CVS calls on Wednesday against $1.51M in puts, and the name reports on Tuesday, October 27.

The stock is up 10.0% in 21 sessions while the S&P lost 0.5%. Now it sits still in a tight band between $94.02 and $95.54, and the money keeps coming in on the call side.

The Flow. This Is Why You're Reading This.

$CVS closed at $94.48 (1.1%). Here is what hit the 2026-11-27 chain.

Strike $94.00 (ATM) : the confirmed bet

  • Open Interest: 132
  • OI Change: +130 contracts
  • Volume: 1
  • Premium (mid): $4.65
  • Delta: 0.5421
  • IV: 37.6%

Open interest jumped by 130 contracts overnight, so the buyer kept the position through the close. This was a position someone chose to hold. 130 contracts held means roughly $60K in premium sitting on the position, controlling 13,000 shares, about $1.23M in notional exposure.

A delta of 0.5421 means the contract gains about 54 cents for every dollar $CVS rises. The buyer picked the strike at the money with an expiry one month past earnings. That is a directional bet on the report and the weeks after it, with enough time to be right late.

Strike $70.00 (ITM) : the unconfirmed signal

  • Volume: 340
  • Open Interest: 0
  • Premium (mid): $23.95

This one sits on the 2026-11-20 expiry and is the largest contract among the near expiries. The volume printed. The open interest has not updated yet, so I cannot tell if the buyer held it or sold it before the bell. About $814K changed hands here.

Watch the OI update tomorrow. That is the tell.

If both signals confirm, the combined picture is 470 contracts, $875K in premium, $4.44M in notional.

The two strikes are part of a bigger stream. Call premium ran 34.1× a normal day, 99% of the premium went to calls, and the net over five sessions comes to $123.62M on the call side.

Where The Dealers Are

Dealers sit above their gamma flip, and that changes how the next moves trade. The call wall at $100.00 is where hedging selling tends to cap a rally. The put wall at $85.00 is where hedging buying tends to catch a drop.

  • Call wall: $100.00
  • Put wall: $85.00
  • Gamma flip: $89.00
  • Regime: stabilizing

Above $89.00, dealers sell into rips and buy into dips. That dampens swings, which explains the tight band of the last sessions. The stop at $89.97 sits just above the flip. A close under it puts dealers on the other side, where their hedging speeds up the fall. My stop and the dealers' switch point are close together on purpose.

What The Options Market Is Paying

  • 30-day IV: 39.7%, rank 97 over the past year
  • 25-delta skew: -1.1%
  • Term structure: front above back, an event or crush premium near term

Volatility on $CVS is close to its most expensive level of the year. A rank of 97 is a level where people sell vol. Buyers pay the earnings premium in full, and the inverted term structure says the market expects that premium to bleed out after Tuesday.

Earnings land on October 27, in 4 days. The stock moves 3.4% on an average report day. Anyone who buys calls today pays for a bigger move than that and needs direction to beat the crush.

Why Now

$CVS trades at 24.3 times trailing earnings and 10.8 times forward earnings. The gap is the story. The Street expects earnings per share to more than double from $3.8. Free cash flow sits at $8.08B (Yahoo) on a $120.8B market cap. The stock trades at 1.51 times its book value of $62.37 per share. Profitability is still the weak point. The recovery shows up in the forecasts, and margins have not caught up yet.

The Street is on board. 25 analysts cover it with a strong buy consensus. The lowest target is $103.0, the average $115.48, the highest $145.0. Every target sits above today's price, and the average is 22% above the close.

Price has done half the work. $CVS closed above its 200-day average at $88.46, 6.8% over it. It still sits well under the $110.68 high of July 22. The March 30 low at $69.51 is far behind. The relative strength confirms it, and the sector helps a little. In the XLV group, 40% of the S&P 500 health names trade above their trend, and that share is broadening. The flow is betting the report closes the gap to the July high.

What They're Targeting

October 27: Q3 earnings. The $94 call needs a move above strike plus premium by November 27. Guidance on Tuesday decides if the forward multiple of 10.8 holds or gets re-rated. A beat with confirmed guidance pushes price toward the $100.00 call wall first.

November 20: expiry of the $70 call. If the open interest confirms tomorrow, that is $3.21M of notional someone wants to keep through the report.

How To Play It

Equity (conservative): Entry $94.48. Stop $89.97 (4.8% risk). Target $105.37 (11.5%). R/R 2.4. Size: Starter, cap around 2%.

The target sits at the overhead supply near the three-month high. The stop is two ATR under entry, below nearby support. You can also wait for a dip toward $94.02, the bottom of the band, for a slightly better fill.

Follow the flow (aggressive): Buy the $94 call expiring 2026-11-27 at about $4.65. At the $105.37 target on expiry, the contract is worth the full gap between $94 and $105.37, more than twice what you paid. Below $94 on expiry, it is worth zero. Max loss = the premium. Size: 1 to 2% of portfolio.

Best of both: Hold the core in shares at $94.48 with the $89.97 stop. Add one small $94 call as a kicker for the earnings move. The shares carry the trade. The call adds upside if Tuesday goes well, and you lose only the premium if it does not.

What Could Go Wrong

A daily close below $89.97 breaks the setup and ends the trade. Under $89.00 the dealers stop absorbing the selling and start adding to it, and the put wall at $85.00 is the next real support.

Volatility is the second risk. With IV rank at 97, a decent report can still crush the call. Theta eats a one-month option every day the stock stays in the band. The flow may also be a hedge. 11 funds added and 13 trimmed at the last quarterly filing, and insiders have been selling. Point72 grew the value of its line by 1447.7% and Viking Global by 100%, while Dodge & Cox, the largest holder at $5.17B, trimmed. A fund that is short the stock elsewhere can buy calls to cover its risk.

Money on the table carries no promise. The big buyer can be wrong, and the report on Tuesday decides it. Size accordingly.

Daniel

The market is paying for the relative strength and ignoring the calendar. Earnings land on November 9, in 13 days. The stock trades at 61.3x forward earnings with a fundamentals score of 31/100. That makes this a momentum trade with a short fuse, and I size it like one.

The Setup

Casella Waste Systems collects trash and recycling, sorts it, and buries what is left in landfills it owns, mostly across the Northeast. A new landfill is hard to get permitted, so the company that owns the hole sets the price. Revenue grew 17% last quarter against the same quarter a year earlier. Much of that came from buying smaller haulers, which is how Casella has grown for years. The earnings have not caught up. Trailing EPS is $0.09, so the trailing P/E reads 977.8. Even on the Street's forward earnings, the stock costs 61.3x, and it trades at 3.93 times its book value of $24.83 a share. Industrials are washed out right now, and waste is the defensive corner of that sector, because people throw things away in every economy. A steady business priced for perfection, with a momentum trade on top.

$CWST peaked at $107.96 on February 11, then fell to $74.05 by March 25. It has rebuilt since. It closed October 23 at $97.61 (0.7% on the session), which is 69% of its 52-week range. That close came after a 16.4% run in 21 sessions, while the S&P lost 0.9%.

I read this chart through volume, because a stock only respects the prices where people actually traded. Right now that trading happens in a narrow band between $97.16 and $98.32. After a 16.4% month, the stock went quiet and kept the move, so buyers are accepting these prices. The problem is overhead. Everyone who bought the February top near $107.96 is still underwater, and many of them will sell to get even around $107.64. That is where I take profit. Underneath, a daily close below $90.92 means the band failed and the buyers walked away. I would buy the low edge of the band at $97.16, and I would not pay up into $98.32 before it breaks. If it reaches $107.64, take the win. With earnings on the calendar, do not wait for a new high.

Fundamentals

Score: 31/100

The Good: revenue grew 17% last quarter year over year. Yahoo shows $121.70M of free cash flow. No pillar of the score is strong. The best is valuation at 38/100, then risk and dilution at 37/100. Growth and balance sheet both sit at 34/100.

The Bad: profitability is the pillar that drags everything down, at 15/100. The app reads the SEC filings over four quarters, and that version shows free cash flow being burned, which contradicts the Yahoo figure. 11% of the float is sold short, and the governance risk score is weak.

The Street is bullish. 10 analysts cover it with a consensus buy. Targets run from $91.0 to $130.0, and the average of $108.4 sits 11.1% above the last close. The 31 splits two ways. Analysts pay for the landfills and the deals, and the score reads an income statement that has caught up with neither.

The Sector

Industrials are in a washout. Only 8% of the S&P 500 industrial names trade above their own trend, and the app puts the group at extreme fear. That share has started to widen again, so the selling is thinning out. $CWST gained 16.4% in 21 sessions in a sector where almost nothing works. That is the kind of strength I want to own before the rest of the group catches up.

Confluence

None of my setup screeners flag $CWST today. Relative strength alone put it on my list: it beat the S&P by 20% over the past month. The trend has not fully turned up yet, so the strength comes before the structure. That is why the plan starts at starter size and waits for the band.

The fund filings show who is behind the move. At the last quarterly filing, 5 funds added and 3 trimmed. Baron Capital is the anchor, with a line worth $93.60M, up 64% in value. AQR more than doubled the value of its line, and Fisher and Two Sigma grew theirs. On the other side, Point72 trimmed a $43.20M line, Marshall Wace cut, and Caxton left. These percentages include the price move, so they measure value and do not count shares bought.

A long-term growth house built its stake while quant shops rotated around it. So the floor is patient money and the swing is fast money. Fast money can leave in a week. That is why I want the band to hold before I add.

Options Flow

The flow is thin, with one exception. Among the near expirations, the largest contract is the November 20 $80 call: 149 contracts, about $197K of premium, 14,900 shares and $1.45M of notional. It sits deep in the money, so the buyer is using it as a substitute for the stock. The trade is unconfirmed until open interest updates. Dealers hold their call wall at $95 and their put wall at $80. The stock sits above the call wall, in a regime where dealer hedging dampens moves. Implied volatility is 44%, and this call expires after the November 9 report. I would still rather own the stock.

How To Play It

Conservative:

Entry: $97.61 to $97.16 (current pullback zone)

Stop: $90.92 (a daily close below breaks the setup)

Target 1: $107.64 (the supply left under the February high)

From $97.61, you risk 6.9% to make 10.3%, about 1.5 to 1. Starter size, capped around 2%.

Aggressive:

Wait for a daily close above $98.32, the top of the band. Buy the break with the same stop and the same target. You pay more per share and the ratio gets worse, but you only own it once the band resolves upward. Use half the size of the conservative line.

What Could Go Wrong

Earnings on November 9 fall inside the holding window. At 61.3x forward earnings, a miss gaps through any stop. 11% of the float is short, so the stock can move fast in both directions. If industrials take another leg down, a name up 16.4% in a month is an easy one to sell. Max allocation 2%, and starter size until the band breaks.

Size accordingly.

Daniel
